A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework, renamed from SYMBOLIC-MOE to SKILL-MOE. All 22 pages of v3 and 20 pages of v4, including figures, tables, equations, and appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: v3 reports original benchmark evaluations, expert-selection and aggregation ablations, transfer experiments, and runtime measurements in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds profile-transfer evaluations, ARC-Challenge results, controlled aggregation comparisons, and failure and skill-distribution analyses.

M1.justification: Section 3.2.1 changes the stated keyword-retention rule: v3 retains keywords appearing more than once across the whole validation set, whereas v4 requires recurrence within each question's annotations. This revises profile construction; the routing scores, aggregator selection, and batching procedure otherwise remain.

E1.justification: v4 adds ARC-Challenge evaluation for less heterogeneous commonsense reasoning (Appendix K) and removes MATH-Hard evaluation from v3 Table 5. The four primary benchmarks and OmniMATH remain, making this a limited revision of supplementary coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 removes GPT4o-mini, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and DeepSeekV3 and adds QwenR1 32B. The principal single-model and multi-agent comparison methods remain. New Table 14 also evaluates three calls to the task-best model followed by the selected aggregator.

E3.justification: v4 adds MMLU-Pro-derived profiles for OmniMATH and matched three-call controls separating expert selection from aggregation. ARC-Challenge uses 299 official validation examples. Section 5.3 specifies three discussion rounds where v3 described 'a round discussion'; the corresponding scores remain identical, so this establishes a reported protocol revision, not a confirmed rerun.

E4.justification: v4 substantially expands diagnostic evidence through expert-versus-aggregator controls (Table 14), quantified collective expert failures and aggregation errors (Appendix L), and skill distributions (Table 11 and Figure 6). Transfer analysis adds MMLU-Pro-to-OmniMATH evaluation while removing MATH-Hard transfer. Existing keyword-LLM sensitivity, trimming, and aggregator analyses are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: Both Appendix C sections state averaging over three random seeds, with the same proprietary-model exception. The existing uncertainty-reporting style is retained; no new confidence intervals, significance tests, or repeated-run procedures are documented.

E6.justification: The method's Table 1 scores, including its 62.43 average, remain unchanged. Substantial new results include OmniMATH accuracy of 49.32 versus Debate's 34.51 using MMLU-Pro profiles, ARC-Challenge accuracy of 91.7 versus MoA's 90.1, QwenR1 32B results, and diagnostic analyses. MATH-Hard and three reference-model result rows disappear. New Table 14 reports GPQA recruited-expert majority voting at 53.34, while retained Table 4 reports 53.54.

T1.justification: The routing and aggregation equations remain equivalent, including Equations 1–2 moved from v3 Appendix M to v4 Appendix S. The added explanation of the functional MoE analogy introduces no new formal assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: v4's introduction drops explicit superiority claims over the named proprietary-model comparisons, and its conclusion describes matching GPT4o-mini rather than outperforming it. The central claims about training-free skill routing, efficient 16-model batching, and the 8.15-point average advantage remain.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations connecting domain-shift resilience to transferable skills, interprets skill labels as meaningful structure, explicitly discusses the batched-arrival assumption, and identifies collective expert and aggregation failures. Conversely, v3's limitations concerning inference cost, possible distillation, and the Keyword LLM's required domain knowledge disappear. Appendix L also asserts noisy-input robustness without describing a corresponding noise experiment.

D1.justification: v4 explicitly discloses sampling experts with replacement and replaces the first-page project link with a labeled code-repository link. The listed GLM4 checkpoint reference changes, without establishing an actual model replacement. Hardware, generation limits, prompts, and principal hyperparameters are otherwise retained.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds positioning against DER, Router-R1, and LLM-Blender; these are cited rather than experimentally evaluated. The separate inference-time-scaling discussion and references such as MAGICoRe and Snell et al. disappear. Most existing MoE and multi-agent positioning remains.

P1.justification: The paper is renamed throughout, the abstract and conclusion are rewritten, and experimental setup becomes a separate section incorporating the former appendix baseline descriptions. Analyses are reordered, discussion and conclusion are separated, and keyword-LLM sensitivity moves to Appendix P. These constitute substantial narrative reorganization beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from single-column presentation to a two-column conference layout, with extensively rearranged tables and captions. Table 1 reorders benchmark columns and categories; the transfer table switches from dataset columns to profile-source columns. Tables 11, 13, and 14 and Figure 6 are new, while Figures 1–5 largely retain their content.

improvement.justification: New matched controls in Table 14 better separate routing and aggregation benefits, while the broader profile-transfer test strengthens generalization evidence. ARC-Challenge and failure analyses also improve assessment of applicability. These modest gains are partly offset by conflicting GPQA voting scores, retained proprietary-model claims after their supporting comparison rows are removed, and loss of the Keyword LLM domain-knowledge caveat.
